stories.head: US carries out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island
stories.stand: US officials said the 'defensive' strikes near the Strait of Hormuz followed Iranian fire, hours after Iran offered to reopen the strait on conditions.
stories.say: The US has carried out what officials called limited defensive strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, hours after Tehran said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz on conditions.
body: US officials said the military carried out limited "defensive" strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday. A senior official told CBS News the strikes hit Qeshm Island.

That official said the strikes followed Iran's Revolutionary Guards firing at an American aircraft. Another US official told ABC the targets were Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets. Iran's IRNA news agency reported several explosions on the island.

Earlier on Monday, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the strait could reopen within two days if the US met its conditions. These include ending the war, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US naval blockade, Euronews reported.

Vice President JD Vance said he and President Donald Trump felt "pretty good" about the prospects for a negotiated settlement. Qatar is mediating between the two sides. No casualty figures have been given.

stories.head: Russian bombs kill 26 at Ukrainian aid centre, Kyiv says
stories.stand: Ukrainian officials said a school used for weekly aid handouts in Komyshuvakha was bombed twice on Monday, and 27 people were still missing.
stories.say: Ukrainian officials say Russian bombs killed at least 26 people at a school used to hand out aid in Komyshuvakha, with a second strike hitting the shelter where people had gathered.
body: Russian aircraft bombed the village of Komyshuvakha in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region on Monday, killing at least 26 people, Ukrainian officials said. The target was a school used to distribute humanitarian aid every week.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the first strike was followed by nine more bombs aimed directly at the shelter where people had gathered. Officials said 27 people were missing.

Ukraine's emergency service said two of its rescuers were among the dead. Police said drones, shelling and thick smoke slowed the search. Regional head Mykhailo Semikin declared Tuesday a day of mourning.
The attack came a day after a US-brokered local ceasefire around Oleshky, in Kherson region, expired. No Russian comment was reported.

stories.head: US to mediate Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi next week
stories.stand: Envoy Steve Witkoff said working-level talks on 10 and 11 November will cover post-war security, de-escalation and humanitarian measures.
stories.say: Steve Witkoff says the US will bring Ukrainian and Russian delegations together in Abu Dhabi on the 10th and 11th of November, after meetings with European allies in Brussels.
body: US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday that the US will mediate talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. He described them as working-level negotiations.

Witkoff said the talks would cover post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures and ending the war. A senior US official told Reuters that Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to lead the US side.

First, US negotiators will meet officials from France, Germany, Britain, the EU and NATO in Brussels this week. Those talks will cover security guarantees for Ukraine and support for its reconstruction.

The last US-mediated talks were held in February, before the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, Reuters reported. Vladimir Putin agreed to the new round after meeting Witkoff in St Petersburg.

stories.head: Netanyahu seeks broad government as opposition backs Eisenkot
stories.stand: Neither bloc has a majority after Israel's election; President Herzog begins consultations on Wednesday and has until 11 November to pick a candidate.
stories.say: Benjamin Netanyahu has called for a broad national government under his leadership without Arab parties, while opposition leaders have lined up behind Gadi Eisenkot.
body: Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday called for a "broad national government" that would exclude Arab parties. He said that as leader of the largest party, Likud, he should lead the next coalition.

Opposition party leaders have endorsed Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister. His bloc won 48 seats in last week's election, against 53 for Netanyahu's camp, in the 120-seat Knesset. Arab-majority lists won a record 19 seats.
The opposition is divided over working with the Arab lists. Yair Golan supports a partnership, while Avigdor Lieberman strongly opposes one.
President Isaac Herzog begins consultations with the parties on Wednesday. He has until 11 November to choose a candidate, who will then have 28 days to form a government.

stories.head: US plans to deport Afghans to Taliban rule via Pakistan
stories.stand: A US official said deportees would fly to Pakistan and be returned to Afghanistan; the Taliban and 66 members of Congress raised concerns.
stories.say: The US plans to deport Afghan detainees by flying them to Pakistan for return to Afghanistan, an official said, drawing concern from the Taliban and 66 members of Congress.
body: The Trump administration plans to deport Afghan nationals held by ICE by flying them to Pakistan, from where they would be returned to Afghanistan, a US official told CBS News. The US has no diplomatic relations with the Taliban government.

An ICE officer said in a sworn court declaration that a charter flight's final destination would be Pakistan, with onward transport to Afghanistan. A flight from Alexandria, Louisiana, had been due on Tuesday, but the official said plans were in flux.

Taliban foreign ministry spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi expressed "serious concern" and urged a responsible approach. 66 members of Congress wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin asking them to cancel the flights.

Advocates say some deportees could face persecution over links to the US war effort. The Department of Homeland Security said people sent to third countries receive notice and assurances before removal.

stories.head: Belgian PM De Wever offers resignation after budget talks collapse
stories.stand: King Philippe is withholding his decision and will consult party leaders, after the five-party coalition failed to agree a 2027 budget.
stories.say: Belgium's prime minister Bart De Wever has offered his resignation after his five-party coalition failed to agree a budget, but King Philippe has yet to decide whether to accept it.
body: Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever offered his resignation to King Philippe on Monday after his five-party coalition failed to agree a 2027 budget. The palace said the king was withholding his decision.
The palace said the king regretted the lack of an agreement that would give the country a credible budget. He will consult party leaders from Tuesday and see De Wever again on Friday.

The coalition split over who should bear more of the burden. Vooruit, CD&V and Les Engagés wanted more from those with the "strongest shoulders", which N-VA and MR opposed. De Wever had sought €10 billion in savings or new revenue.
Belgium's deficit is 5.2% of GDP, the highest in the eurozone, the Brussels Times reported. De Wever wants to avoid a stopgap system of monthly budgets based on this year's spending.

stories.head: Uganda begins pulling troops out of Somalia after almost 20 years
stories.stand: Uganda's army said the first troops are home and all forces will leave by the end of 2027, handing security to Somalia's army.
stories.say: Uganda's army says it has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades, with the first soldiers already home and a full exit due by the end of 2027.
body: Uganda's army said on Monday it had begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia, ending almost 20 years of operations there. Army spokesman Colonel Chris Magezi said the first group had already returned home.

Troops deployed under a bilateral deal with Somalia's government will leave first, within days. Ugandans serving in the African Union mission, known as AUSSOM, will follow gradually, with all forces out by the end of 2027.
Uganda was the first country to join the African Union mission, in 2007, and provides about 40% of its force, AFP reported. The army said Somalia's forces would take full responsibility for security.
Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked group, still controls large parts of central Somalia. The US has said it will stop funding a UN logistics mission that supports African Union forces.

stories.head: Taiwan detects 49 Chinese military aircraft, the most this year
stories.stand: Taiwan's defence ministry said 31 of the aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line, beating this year's previous daily high of 42.
stories.say: Taiwan says it detected 49 Chinese military aircraft around the island in 24 hours, the highest daily count this year, with 31 crossing the median line of the Taiwan Strait.
body: Taiwan's defence ministry said on Tuesday it had detected 49 Chinese military aircraft around the island in a 24-hour period. It is the highest daily figure so far in 2026, according to the EFE news agency.

The ministry said 31 of the aircraft crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait and entered parts of Taiwan's air defence identification zone. They included bombers, fighters, drones and helicopters.
The previous high this year was 42 aircraft, on 13 February. The surge comes as dozens of Chinese ships are deployed in the western Pacific, including a carrier group led by the Liaoning.
China claims Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out using force to take control of it. No Chinese statement on the flights was reported.

stories.head: Rubio presses Venezuela on phased plan in first talks with new minister
stories.stand: Meeting Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco, the US reaffirmed a three-phase plan ending in a democratic transition and urged more prisoner releases.
stories.say: Marco Rubio has held his first meeting with Venezuela's new foreign minister, Oliver Blanco, urging Caracas to stick to a three-phase plan that ends in a democratic transition.
body: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Venezuela's new foreign minister, Oliver Blanco, at the State Department on Monday. It was their first official meeting since the two countries restored relations, El Tiempo reported.

A State Department readout reaffirmed President Donald Trump's three-phase plan for Venezuela: stabilisation, economic recovery and political reconciliation, then democratic transition. Rubio also urged faster releases of political prisoners.
No election date has been set. Opposition leader María Corina Machado said Rubio had set out steps that made clear presidential elections would be held in 2027.
Acting President Delcy Rodríguez appointed Blanco last week. US forces seized former president Nicolás Maduro in January and took him to the US to face charges.

stories.head: Truck bomb near Colombian military base kills four, including baby
stories.stand: Officials said a dump truck loaded with explosives blew up in Planadas, Tolima, on Sunday night, killing four civilians.
stories.say: A truck bomb near a military base in the Colombian town of Planadas has killed four civilians, including a two-month-old baby, officials say.
body: A dump truck loaded with explosives blew up near a military base in Planadas, in Colombia's Tolima department, on Sunday night. Officials said four civilians were killed, including a two-month-old baby.
El Tiempo reported that 18 people were wounded and 177 homes damaged, and that a hospital red alert was declared. Mayor Juan Camilo Hueje imposed a curfew.

Tolima's governor, Adriana Matiz, called the attack "a vile and criminal act". El Tiempo said military intelligence blamed an alliance of two FARC dissident fronts, while the Rio Times reported that no group had claimed it.
President Abelardo De La Espriella called for reinforced military operations in Planadas, and the army sent two platoons, El Tiempo reported.

stories.head: North Korea tests cruise missile with dispersal warhead
stories.stand: State media said Monday's test improved a vertical strike capability; Seoul said it was analysing the launch with Washington.
stories.say: North Korea says it tested a strategic cruise missile carrying a dispersal warhead on Monday, a day after it reported a test of cluster bomb warheads.
body: North Korea test-fired a strategic cruise missile carrying a dispersal warhead on Monday, the state news agency KCNA reported on Tuesday. It said the test assessed the missile's ability to make a vertical strike.
The test came a day after the North reported testing cluster bomb warheads. KCNA said the test improved the missile's manoeuvrability as it approaches its target.
South Korea's military did not announce the launch. A spokesperson for its Joint Chiefs of Staff said Seoul and Washington were analysing the missile in detail.
Unlike ballistic missile launches, cruise missile tests are not banned by UN Security Council sanctions. Tensions have risen since a landmine blast on the border wounded three South Korean soldiers.

stories.head: First Algerian troop convoy reaches Niger escorting fuel tankers
stories.stand: About 60 fuel tankers escorted by Algerian soldiers reached Agadez, a week after Algeria's parliament approved sending troops to Niger.
stories.say: A convoy of about 60 fuel tankers escorted by Algerian soldiers has reached Agadez in northern Niger, a week after Algeria's parliament approved sending troops there.
body: A first convoy of Algerian soldiers escorting about 60 fuel tankers reached Agadez in northern Niger on Saturday, RFI reported. Nigerien forces met the convoy at the border.
Algeria's parliament approved sending troops to Niger on 25 October. Africanews described it as Algeria's first military deployment abroad since the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.

Officially, the convoy provides logistical support amid strained fuel supplies in Niger. President Abdelmadjid Tebboune said the deployment responded to national security considerations and was part of cooperation with Niamey.

Algerian soldiers are expected to help Niger fight armed groups along the shared border, Africanews reported. RFI said an Algerian unit could also be stationed in Niamey. No troop numbers have been given.

stories.head: French pupils resume school blockades after half-term break
stories.stand: Dozens of schools were blockaded as students returned on Monday, with a Paris march planned for Tuesday and a cross-sector strike on Thursday.
stories.say: High school students in France resumed blockading dozens of schools on Monday as classes restarted after a two-week break, demanding more teachers and smaller classes.
body: High school students in France resumed protests on Monday as schools reopened after a two-week break, Al Jazeera reported. Dozens of schools were blockaded, though on a smaller scale than before the holiday.

Before the break, more than 160 high schools in the Paris region were fully or partly closed on the busiest days, according to Sortiraparis. Students are demanding more teachers, smaller classes, school renovations and changes to the Parcoursup admissions system.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced a €5 billion renovation plan and a Parcoursup overhaul on 26 October. Student groups said the timeline was too slow.
A student march in Paris is planned for Tuesday. Unions including the CGT and CFDT have called a cross-sector strike over wages, pensions and public services on Thursday.

stories.head: Two teenagers arrested over Halloween party stabbings in Hampshire
stories.say: Two teenagers from Southampton have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after five boys were stabbed at a Halloween party in Chandler's Ford; one is critically hurt.
stories.stand: A 16-year-old and a 17-year-old are in custody; one of the five injured boys remains in a life-threatening condition.
body: Police have arrested two teenagers, aged 16 and 17 and both from Southampton, on suspicion of attempted murder after five boys were stabbed at a Halloween party in Chandler's Ford, Hampshire.

Officers were called just after 10.30pm on Saturday to a supervised party at an address in Park Road. Police said uninvited males got into the garden through a fence and attacked guests in the garden and nearby roads.
The injured boys are three 16-year-olds and two 17-year-olds. Two remain in hospital, one of them a 17-year-old in a life-threatening condition. The other three have been discharged.

Detective Chief Inspector Elizabeth Pirie called the arrests a significant development and urged anyone with information or footage to come forward. Barton Peveril college said two of the injured were believed to be its students.

stories.head: UK troops to rehearse post-war Ukraine mission in Poland
stories.say: About 300 British personnel will join 2,800 troops from 11 countries in Poland this month to rehearse how a multinational force could support Ukraine once fighting stops.
stories.stand: Exercise Koalicja, led by Britain and France, runs from 9 to 22 November and is the first major test of the Multinational Force Ukraine.
body: About 300 UK personnel will take part in Exercise Koalicja in Poland from 9 to 22 November, the Ministry of Defence said. Some 2,800 troops from 11 countries will train on land, at sea and in the air.

It is the first major exercise of the Multinational Force Ukraine, the military arm of the Coalition of the Willing, which Britain and France lead. It is commanded by British Lieutenant General Tom Bateman.

Soldiers from 7 Brigade will rehearse moving troops and supplies. RAF Typhoons and a Voyager tanker will practise protecting commercial flights once Ukraine's airspace reopens. Turkish forces in Istanbul will test mine clearance for shipping.

The ministry said the force would enter Ukraine only after fighting ends and at Kyiv's request, and would not do peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the UK was preparing for the day peace comes.

stories.head: Russell Brand's lawyer tells jury 2023 reporting 'poisoned the well'
stories.say: Russell Brand's barrister has told jurors that media coverage in 2023 compromised the case against him; Brand denies three counts of rape and four other sexual offences.
stories.stand: Ian Winter KC gave the defence closing speech at Southwark Crown Court; Brand denies all seven charges involving six women.
body: Russell Brand's barrister, Ian Winter KC, gave his closing speech at Southwark Crown Court on Monday. Brand, 51, denies three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.
The charges involve six women, and the allegations span about a decade from 1999.

Mr Winter argued that a 2023 Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and reporting by The Times and The Sunday Times had compromised the case. He told jurors it was not criminal to treat women unkindly if there was consent.
He argued that the complainants' accounts showed Brand believed they had consented. The trial continues.

stories.say: Nine men have gone on trial in Manchester accused of sexual offences against a woman whose husband, prosecutors say, drugged her and shared footage of the abuse online.
stories.stand: The trial opened at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday; all nine men deny the charges, which include rape and conspiracy to rape.
body: Nine men aged 28 to 70 went on trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday. They are accused of sexual offences against a woman whose husband drugged and abused her. All nine deny the charges.

The charges include rape, conspiracy to rape, assault by penetration and administering a substance. The husband, a man in his 60s from Stockport, pleaded guilty in September to offences including rape. He cannot be named to protect his wife's anonymity, and will be sentenced later.

Opening the case, Louise Oakley KC said the husband drugged his wife and abused her while she was unconscious. She said he filmed the abuse and shared it online, and that other men advised him on how to incapacitate her.
The prosecution said the defendants knew the woman was not conscious and not consenting. Four other men have pleaded guilty to various offences.

stories.head: Record 757 officers barred from policing in England and Wales
stories.say: A record 757 police officers in England and Wales were added to the barred list in 2025 to 26, the College of Policing says, with dishonesty the most common reason.
stories.stand: College of Policing figures show the highest annual total since the barred list began in 2017, up from 735 the year before.
body: A record 757 police officers in England and Wales were added to the barred list in 2025/26, College of Policing figures show. That is up from 735 in 2024/25 and 594 in 2023/24.
It is the highest annual total since the list began in December 2017. Of those barred, 334 were serving officers, 397 had resigned and 26 had retired.

Dishonesty was the most common reason, cited 142 times, followed by discriminatory behaviour at 110 and unlawful access or disclosure of information at 101. Sexual offences or misconduct featured in 87 cases. Some cases had more than one reason.
Assistant Chief Constable Arman Mathieson of the College of Policing said the total was about 0.5% of serving officers and that the service would act when trust was broken.

stories.head: UK and Germany agree to develop missiles with 2,000km range
stories.say: Britain and Germany have agreed to jointly develop precision strike weapons with a range of more than 2,000 kilometres, after defence ministers met in Berlin on Monday.
stories.stand: Wes Streeting and Boris Pistorius also signed off joint work on Sting Ray torpedoes, AI and space at the second UK-Germany Defence Ministerial Council.
body: Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius met in Berlin on Monday for the second Defence Ministerial Council under the 2024 Trinity House Agreement.

In a joint statement, they committed to developing Deep Precision Strike capabilities with ranges over 2,000km, due within the decade. Pistorius said talks with industry were under way and other European partners could join.

The two countries' armaments directors signed an arrangement on buying the Sting Ray torpedo. The ministers also agreed to extend a joint cyber project to artificial intelligence, and to begin closer work on defence space.
Pistorius said relations between the two countries were at an all-time high.

stories.say: A Wizz Air flight from Luton to Sofia was diverted to Budapest on Monday after a bomb threat, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet; nothing suspicious was found on board.
stories.stand: A Hungarian Gripen escorted the plane to Budapest, where checks of the aircraft and passengers found nothing, reports said.
body: A Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia in Bulgaria was diverted to Budapest on Monday after a bomb threat was received during the flight.
A Hungarian Gripen fighter jet escorted the aircraft to Budapest Liszt Ferenc International Airport, Hungary's defence minister said. The plane landed safely and taxied to a designated stand.

Wizz Air said it landed in line with security protocols and that it was cooperating with the authorities. The aircraft and passengers were checked, and nothing suspicious was found, according to reports. No arrests have been reported.

stories.head: Record subsidence claims after summer heatwaves, insurers say
stories.say: Insurers received a record 13,000 home subsidence claims between July and September after the summer heatwaves, up from 8,000 a year earlier, the Association of British Insurers says.
stories.stand: The average subsidence payout held at a record £20,000, and the ABI says new homes must be built to cope with extreme weather.
body: Members of the Association of British Insurers received a record 13,000 new domestic subsidence claims between July and September, after the summer heatwaves. That compares with 8,000 in the same period last year.
The average subsidence payout stayed at a record £20,000 for a second quarter in a row. The ABI advised homeowners to seek help if cracks wider than 3mm appear, especially diagonal or sudden ones.

Across home and business property, claims fell 4% on the previous quarter to 142,000, but payouts rose 1% to £1.5 billion. The average payout hit a record £10,000, which the ABI linked to repair costs and severe weather.
Chris Bose of the ABI said more action was needed to prevent damage, and that new homes should be built to withstand extreme weather. The average home insurance premium was £329.

stories.head: Charities urge PM to lift housing benefit freeze for private renters
stories.say: Nineteen charities, including Shelter and the Trussell Trust, have urged Andy Burnham to end the freeze on housing benefit for private renters, warning it will push families into poverty.
stories.stand: An open letter cites Joseph Rowntree Foundation estimates that nearly 200,000 families could be pushed into poverty or deeper hardship.
body: Nineteen organisations, including the Trussell Trust, Shelter, Generation Rent and the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, have written to Prime Minister Andy Burnham urging him to end the freeze on Local Housing Allowance.
The allowance sets housing benefit for private renters and has been frozen since April 2024. The letter says the gap between benefit rates and rents reached a record 23.3% in October.
Citing Joseph Rowntree Foundation research, the charities say nearly 200,000 families could be pushed into poverty or deeper hardship. They say restoring support would cost £1.7bn.
A government spokesperson said more than £40bn was being invested in affordable and social housing, and that the Renters' Rights Act protects tenants from unfair rent rises.

stories.head: Former Police Scotland sergeant jailed for rapes lodges appeal
stories.say: Campbell Petrie, a former Police Scotland sergeant jailed last month for raping two women, has lodged notice that he intends to appeal against his conviction and sentence.
stories.stand: The Crown Office confirmed the 50-year-old's intention to appeal; his full grounds are due by 22 December.
body: Campbell Petrie, a former Police Scotland sergeant, has lodged an intention to appeal against his conviction and sentence, the Crown Office confirmed. A note setting out his grounds is due by 22 December.
Petrie, 50, was found guilty in September of offences against two women in Glasgow, including rape and indecent assault. The offences took place between 2006 and 2022, while he was a serving officer.

In October, at the High Court in Glasgow, Judge Alistair Watson gave him an extended sentence of 15 years, with 12 years in custody. The judge said the crimes caused the victims deep and enduring psychological harm.
Petrie was suspended in December 2023 and retired from the force in December 2025.

stories.head: Karl Bushby walks into Hull after 28 years on foot around the world
stories.say: Former paratrooper Karl Bushby has walked into Hull to cheering crowds, ending a journey of about 31,000 miles on foot that he began in southern Chile in 1998.
stories.stand: The 57-year-old arrived in Victoria Square on Monday after a walk that crossed the Darien Gap and the frozen Bering Strait.
body: Karl Bushby, a 57-year-old former paratrooper, arrived on foot in Victoria Square in Hull on Monday, ending a walk of about 31,000 miles that took 28 years.

He set out from southern Chile in 1998, aiming to walk home without motorised transport. He had expected the journey to take 12 years. Delays included visa refusals, the 2008 financial crash and Covid.

His route took him through the Darien Gap and across the frozen Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia. He swam the Caspian Sea in 2024, and later swam the Channel after being refused permission to walk through the tunnel.
He was welcomed by Hull's Lord Mayor, Maria Coward. Bushby told the crowd there had never been a welcome home like it.

body: The Department for Transport has published a transport resilience strategy, setting out its approach for the next 5 to 10 years. Minister Keir Mather announced it in a written statement to Parliament on Monday.
The strategy makes 22 practical commitments. They include a new training scheme, the Transport Resilience Academy, and a sector-wide network to share evidence and tackle common risks.

Mather said the strategy builds on the government's July 2025 resilience action plan. He described the threats facing transport as increasingly complex and unpredictable. The statement gave no funding figures.

stories.head: Americans vote in midterms with control of Congress at stake
stories.say: Americans are choosing all 435 members of the House and 35 senators on Tuesday, with Democrats needing a net gain of four seats in each chamber to take control.
stories.stand: All 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships are being contested, with Republicans defending narrow majorities in both chambers.
body: Americans are voting on Tuesday in midterm elections that will decide control of Congress. All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are being contested, along with governorships in 36 states.

Republicans hold 53 Senate seats to the Democrats' 47. In the House, CBS News counts 218 Republicans plus an independent who usually votes with them, against 214 Democrats, with two vacancies. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in each chamber to win control, Euronews reported.

CBS News identified 11 key Senate races, eight in Republican-held seats including Texas, Ohio, Maine and Alaska, and three in Democratic-held Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire. More than 54 million Americans had already voted early, according to the University of Florida Voting Lab.
Polls close at different times across the country. The first results are expected after East Coast polls close, overnight in Europe.

stories.say: Donald Trump closed the midterm campaign beside the Lincoln Memorial on Monday, spending much of a 54-minute speech on the renovated Reflecting Pool and other building projects.
stories.stand: Trump's closing pitch before the midterms centred on his makeover of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool rather than the cost of living.
body: Donald Trump gave his final speech before the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington on Monday. The 54-minute address focused largely on the pool's renovation and other building projects, the Jerusalem Post reported.

Trump said he wanted to hold the event to show how beautiful the pool was, CBS News reported. The administration had announced in April that it would resurface the pool and paint it blue at his request.

After it reopened, the water turned green and paint peeled. Trump said, without evidence, that the pool had been vandalised. The Justice Department later blamed a botched installation by the contractor in a court filing, and charges were dropped against a man accused of damaging it.
Trump called Democrats unfit to serve and noted that sitting presidents tend to lose midterms. On Sunday he held his last rallies in Dubuque, Iowa, and Salina, Kansas.

stories.head: Supreme Court rejects bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
stories.say: The Supreme Court has refused a Trump administration request to make California set aside mail ballots from about 20,000 people it says are likely not citizens.
stories.stand: The court turned down the Justice Department's emergency request on Monday, after two lower courts had already refused it.
body: The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an emergency request from the Trump administration to make California set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 people. The Justice Department says they are likely noncitizens.

The administration argued that once unlawful ballots were counted with valid ones, the harm could not be undone. California said the federal list was unreliable and could wrongly exclude eligible citizens.
A federal judge in Los Angeles, David Carter, had refused the request, saying the identification process was full of uncertainty and errors. A divided appeals court also declined it on Friday.

Separately, Chief Judge James Boasberg in Washington blocked the administration from making requests of California over its mail ballots, Fox News reported. Confirmed cases of noncitizen voting are rare, CBS News noted.

stories.stand: Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui dismissed the complaint against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides from the bench on Monday.
body: A federal magistrate judge in Washington on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides. They were accused of lying to Congress in 2023 about the FBI's handling of Hunter Biden's laptop.
Judge Zia Faruqui said what had happened could only be described as weaponisation. He called the case a rush job directed by President Donald Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel, Fox News reported.
The judge questioned why prosecutors used a complaint rather than seeking a grand jury indictment. He also criticised them for adding a charge without first clearing it with the court.
The case was brought about two weeks before the midterm elections, PBS reported. The Justice Department may still seek an indictment from a grand jury. No department response was reported.

Democrats led Republicans by 46% to 38% when respondents were asked which party's candidate they preferred for Congress. A week earlier the Democratic lead had been 11 points, Daily Maverick reported.

body: Final New York Times/Siena polls of likely voters, released on Sunday, showed Democratic candidates ahead in seven closely watched Senate races. Surveys ran from 23 October to 1 November, Fox News reported.
In Texas, James Talarico led Ken Paxton by 50% to 43%. In Maine, Troy Jackson led Senator Susan Collins by 51% to 45%. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed led Mike Rogers by 53% to 42%.
The closest races were Iowa, where Josh Turek led Ashley Hinson by 48% to 47%, and Alaska, where Mary Peltola led Senator Dan Sullivan by 48% to 46%. Democrats also led in Kansas and Ohio.
Don Levy of the Siena Research Institute cautioned that a Senate majority for either party remained possible. Republicans currently hold the chamber by 53 seats to 47.

stories.say: Shabana Mahmood has set a ten-year standard route to settlement for most migrants, but care workers who arrived before May 2025 keep their five-year path.
stories.stand: The Home Secretary's earned settlement plan sets waits of three to 20 years, with an exemption for care workers after a backlash from Labour MPs.
body: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood told Parliament on Monday that most migrants will face a ten-year route to settlement, including everyone earning under £50,000. Those with a criminal record, poor English, unpaid debts or under three years of National Insurance will be refused.

Higher earners and doctors, nurses and teachers can settle after five years, and those earning over £125,000 after three. People who breach immigration rules face 20 years, and refugees arriving by small boat face longer still.

Care workers who arrived before the May 2025 white paper and met their visa conditions keep a five-year route. About a quarter of the 250,000 who arrived from 2022 to 2025 did not, and will get a new five-year care visa.
City AM said the plans had been softened after criticism from Labour MPs and cabinet ministers. Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said Mahmood had damaged her tough reputation.

stories.say: Andy Burnham says he has not made things harder for the King by opening talks on a slavery apology, ahead of a Commonwealth summit in Antigua where he will pledge £40 million in aid.
stories.stand: The prime minister met the King in Antigua before a Commonwealth summit expected to be dominated by calls for an apology and reparations.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has denied that his offer of talks on a formal slavery apology has made things difficult for King Charles. Asked by ITV News, he said they were reaching out and listening.

The two met on Monday in Antigua before the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, which the King opens on Tuesday. Burnham has ruled out reparations and would not say whether the King should apologise personally.

Buckingham Palace said the King respected talks between governments and it would not be right for him to comment on policy. Africanews reported that his speech would address Britain's role in slavery with unflinching honesty.

LBC reported that Burnham will pledge £40 million over three years for Caribbean infrastructure and set out a debt reset. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch opposes an apology, saying it could open the door to reparations.

stories.say: The Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council, Dan Harrison, has resigned after recordings leaked of him discussing redundancies and saying he wanted to look at women.
stories.stand: Dan Harrison stepped down on Monday after recordings from a private Reform group meeting were leaked online.
body: Dan Harrison, the Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council, resigned on Monday. Recordings from a private meeting of the council's Reform group had been leaked on social media.

In them he is heard discussing making 76 council solicitors redundant and saying he wanted to look at the women next. He apologised unreservedly to staff, saying the remarks were made in a heated private meeting.

Harrison said he had given no instructions to officers and rejected any suggestion that staffing decisions were based on gender. His deputy, Kevin Crook, becomes acting leader until the council elects a successor.
Hours before he quit, all 15 Conservative councillors sought an extraordinary meeting to remove him. Conservative group leader Deborah Taylor said his position had become untenable.

stories.head: Labour ends council power-sharing with Greens over Zionism motion
stories.say: Labour is pulling out of power-sharing deals with the Greens on 11 English councils after Green groups failed to disown a conference motion calling Zionism racism.
stories.stand: Labour withdrew from 11 local arrangements after a Sunday deadline for Green groups to reject their party's October motion.
body: Labour has ended power-sharing arrangements with the Green Party on 11 English councils, including Sheffield, Warwick and West Devon. Local Green groups that did not disown a motion calling Zionism a form of racism were told cooperation would end.

The motion was passed at the Green Party conference in October. Labour chair Bridget Phillipson said it crossed a line and Labour could not work with any party that supported it, the Jewish Chronicle reported.
Green leader Zack Polanski called the motion imperfect but will not seek to overturn it, the paper said. He plans an amendment in 2027.
Israel's foreign ministry called the resolution antisemitic, and Foreign Minister Gideon Saar barred Polanski from entering Israel, AFP reported via Arab News.

stories.head: Reserve Bank of Australia raises rates to 18-year high
stories.say: Australia's central bank has raised its cash rate by a quarter of a point to 4.85%, its fifth rise this year, in a split vote after inflation climbed to 4.3%.
stories.stand: The Reserve Bank of Australia lifted its cash rate to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since 2008, and left the door open to more rises.
body: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.85% on Tuesday. It is the fifth increase this year and takes the rate to its highest level since 2008, ABC News reported.

The decision was not unanimous: six board members backed the rise and three wanted no change, the bank's statement said. It now expects inflation to stay above 3% for the coming year and not reach the top of its target range until late 2027.
Governor Michele Bullock said it was probably good to wait and assess incoming data, Investinglive reported. The Australian dollar fell about 0.3% against the US dollar.

Headline inflation rose to 4.3% in the year to September, from 4.0% in August, ABC News reported. The bank cited oil supply disruptions from the Middle East conflict as a risk. The next decision is due on 8 December.

body: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets on Thursday 5 November, with a quarter-point rise from 3.75% to 4% widely expected. It would be the first increase in three years.

Lenders are competing hard for borrowers. Lloyds finance chief William Chalmers said mortgage margins had been squeezed to about 75 basis points above wholesale costs, City AM reported. NatWest's chief executive said customers were moving towards two-year fixes.
Bank of England data showed mortgage approvals fell to 53,443 in September, a near three-year low. UK Finance says 2.3m households will come to the end of fixed-rate deals in 2027.
Three of the committee's nine members voted for a rise in September. Inflation stands at 3.5%, according to The Negotiator.

stories.head: US to drop South Africa and Rwanda from duty-free trade scheme
stories.say: Washington says it will suspend South Africa and Rwanda from its African duty-free trade programme from January, citing trade barriers and threats to US interests.
stories.stand: The US Trade Representative said the two countries would lose AGOA benefits from 1 January 2027, a move South Africa had prepared for.
body: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Monday that South Africa and Rwanda would be suspended from the African Growth and Opportunity Act from 1 January 2027. The scheme gives eligible African countries duty-free access to the US.

The US said both governments' practices were inconsistent with the scheme's rules. It cited trade and investment barriers in South Africa and threats to US security and foreign policy interests. For Rwanda, it cited trade barriers, rule of law and human rights.
South Africa was the scheme's largest beneficiary, with about $1.7bn of goods sent to the US under it in 2025, down from $4bn in 2024. That is about 1% of its global exports.
Trade Minister Parks Tau said the economy would remain stable and the country would seek other markets. Rwanda's foreign minister said it should not be a scapegoat for events in DR Congo.

body: Apple said on Monday that revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn in the quarter to 26 September, a record for that period. Diluted earnings per share rose 14% to $2.10.
It was the first set of results under chief executive John Ternus. Finance chief Kevan Parekh said net income and earnings per share were September-quarter records.

stories.head: Ryanair half-year profit falls 15% as fuel costs bite
stories.say: Ryanair's first-half profit fell 15% to 2.15 billion euros as fares dipped and fuel costs rose, and Michael O'Leary warned jet fuel prices could stay high well into 2027.
stories.stand: Europe's biggest budget airline reported lower half-year profit on Monday and said it faces a fuel bill about €2bn higher next financial year.
body: Ryanair said on Monday that after-tax profit for the six months to September fell 15% to €2.15bn, RTÉ reported. Passenger numbers rose 6% to 125.8 million, but average fares fell 4%.

Chief executive Michael O'Leary said that unless the Middle East conflict is resolved swiftly, jet fuel prices would stay high well into 2027. The airline expects its fuel bill to rise by about €2bn in the year to March 2028.
About 80% of its fuel is hedged until March 2027, but only 25% for the following year. Ryanair expects higher fares next year but said they were unlikely to cover the full increase.
The airline is reviewing costs, including airport charges and possible temporary pay freezes, and plans greater use of AI. It gave no full-year profit guidance.

stories.stand: A BCC survey found many exporters still face EU customs paperwork and delays, ahead of a UK-EU summit on 20 November.
body: The British Chambers of Commerce said on Monday that the UK's trading relationship with the EU needs to change. It urged ministers to study a range of options and publish detailed comparisons of their economic impact.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham will attend a summit in Brussels on 20 November, LBC reported. He wants deals on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility.

body: Shares in Banque du Caire, one of Egypt's state-owned banks, began trading on the Egyptian Exchange on Monday. Majority shareholder Banque Misr sold 45% of the bank, raising 36.37 billion Egyptian pounds.

stories.stand: A Paris commercial court opened a reorganisation procedure for the company behind BHV Marais on Monday, giving it six months to find a way forward.
body: The Paris economic activities court opened a court-supervised reorganisation for SEGM BHV, the company behind the BHV Marais department store, on Monday, L'Express reported.
The observation period lasts six months and can be renewed once. The court can then approve a recovery plan or a sale, or order liquidation.

As of 26 October, debts due stood at €120.2m against available assets of €410,000. The company had cash-flow problems, was accused of not paying suppliers and faced criticism over a partnership with Shein.
Its managers took over the business from Frédéric Merlin's Société des grands magasins in June. They say the store will stay open.

stories.say: China plans a Mengzhou crew capsule test in 2027, a lunar lander trial in 2028 and a full rehearsal in 2029, before trying to land two astronauts on the Moon in 2030.
stories.stand: A senior designer outlined a year-by-year path to China's first crewed lunar landing at a space symposium in Beijing.
body: China has set out a sequence of test missions leading to its first crewed Moon landing, which it aims to achieve before 2030. The plan was presented by Wang Xiang, a senior designer, at the 7th Manned Space Symposium in Beijing at the weekend.

Two Long March-10 rockets would launch the Lanyue lunar lander and the Mengzhou crew spacecraft separately. They would dock in lunar orbit, and two of three astronauts would then fly down to the surface.

A slide from the presentation, reported by SpacePolicyOnline, showed a Mengzhou test flight to Earth orbit in 2027, a Lanyue landing test in 2028, a full rehearsal in 2029 and a crewed landing in 2030.
The uncrewed lander flight would test launch, lunar orbit entry, docking, landing and take-off, according to Leonard David. NASA has said it aims to land astronauts first, in 2028.

stories.head: Traces of red blood cells reported in 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone
stories.say: Researchers say they have found traces of heme inside fossilised red blood cells in the leg bones of a feathered Brazilian dinosaur, though one outside expert remains unconvinced.
stories.stand: A study in PNAS reports chemical signs of heme in cell-like structures in the bones of Aratasaurus, a Brazilian theropod.
body: Scientists say they have found chemical traces of heme, the iron-containing molecule in haemoglobin, inside fossilised red blood cells in a 115-million-year-old dinosaur. The study was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The bones belong to Aratasaurus museunacionali, a feathered meat-eating dinosaur about 3.1 metres long, found in a mine in north-east Brazil. The structures sat in the vascular canals of its leg bones.

The lead author, Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Perth, said no one had found heme inside a fossil blood cell before. She stressed the team had not found dinosaur DNA, and tests for it were negative.

Independent experts were divided. Mauricio Barbi of the University of Regina found the evidence convincing. Mary Schweitzer of North Carolina State University accepted the heme but doubted the blood cell identification.

stories.head: Hubble finds small galaxies lose most of the oxygen their stars make
stories.say: A Hubble study of 37 nearby dwarf galaxies found they keep only about 11% of the oxygen their stars produce, suggesting winds from exploding stars blow much of it away.
stories.stand: NASA says winds from exploding stars strip oxygen from low-mass galaxies more effectively than current models predict.
body: A study of 37 nearby dwarf galaxies using the Hubble Space Telescope has found that they retain only a small share of the oxygen made by their stars, NASA said on 2 November.
The results, published in The Astrophysical Journal, come from the GLOW project, which stands for Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds. It is funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation.
The team's paper says the galaxies kept between 4% and 25% of their oxygen, about 11% on average. Simulations predict much higher retention, and the researchers blame supernova-driven winds.

It is not yet clear whether the missing oxygen sits in gas around the galaxies or has escaped entirely. The principal investigator is Kristen Wingfield McQuinn of the Space Telescope Science Institute and Rutgers University.

body: Researchers in the Czech Republic and Spain say they have shown for the first time that an altermagnet can act as a source of spin current. The work was published in Nature on 28 October and announced on 2 November.
Altermagnets are a recently identified class of magnets with zero net magnetisation. The team used thin films of a manganese-silicon compound, Mn5Si3, in devices called lateral spin valves.
The group is led by Helena Reichlová at the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences, with Fèlix Casanova at CIC nanoGUNE in San Sebastián.
Altermagnets could in principle lead to smaller, more efficient spintronic devices. Reichlová described the study as fundamental research and said practical uses were a later step.

stories.say: A distant icy object called 2026 ED138, up to 930 miles wide and farther out than Pluto, could be among the largest dwarf planets in its region if follow-up observations confirm it.
stories.stand: The trans-Neptunian object was found in Vera C. Rubin Observatory data in a crowded star field near the Milky Way.
body: Astronomers have found a possible new dwarf planet beyond Pluto using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile. The object, 2026 ED138, was announced on 27 October.
It is estimated at 600 to 1,500 kilometres, or 370 to 930 miles, across. It lies about 46 times as far from the Sun as Earth, beyond Pluto's average distance.

Matthew Holman of the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard and Smithsonian, spotted it on 13 October using software that links detections of moving objects. It had hidden in a star-dense region near the Milky Way.
Further observations, including in infrared, are needed to confirm its size and whether it qualifies as a dwarf planet. Holman said it would join a very small family of worlds if confirmed.

stories.say: NASA's two ESCAPADE spacecraft will fire their engines over southern Australia on the 7th and 9th of November, in a powered flyby of Earth that sends them on to Mars.
stories.stand: The twin probes, launched in November 2025, return to Earth for gravity-assist burns and are due at Mars in September 2027.
body: NASA's twin ESCAPADE spacecraft will make powered flybys of Earth on 7 and 9 November, the agency said on 2 November. Each will fire its engine for about nine minutes over southern Australia.
Closest approach will be between 600 and 1,100 miles above Earth. The burns will raise each probe's speed from about 6.3 to 6.7 miles per second.
The probes launched in November 2025 and have since waited in a loop near a point about a million miles from Earth. NASA says no Mars-bound spacecraft has flown this kind of manoeuvre before.
They are due to reach Mars on 7 and 9 September 2027. There they will fly in formation to study how the solar wind strips away the Martian atmosphere.

stories.head: Theorists find narrow route for a black hole to split in two
stories.say: Physicists say a black hole spinning close to its maximum rate might, in theory, split into smaller black holes, though no such split has ever been observed.
stories.stand: A theoretical study in Physical Review D finds that only very fast-spinning black holes could split without breaking the laws of thermodynamics.
body: A theoretical study suggests a black hole could in principle split into two, but only under extreme conditions. The paper, published in Physical Review D, calls the shape a pair-of-pants topology.

For a non-spinning black hole, splitting would reduce total entropy, breaking the second law of thermodynamics. Rapid spin changes the balance, because spin could turn into the fragments' orbital motion.
The fragments must also fly apart rather than fall back together. That requirement leaves a window only for black holes spinning near their maximum possible rate, the authors found.
A co-author, Francesco Sannino, said no single probability could yet be given. No black hole has been seen to split, and the researchers suggest gamma-ray telescopes could look for signs.

stories.head: Nine-month search finds no blue whales around the Galápagos
stories.say: Researchers who spent nine months searching for blue whales around the Galápagos found none, and suspect unusually warm El Niño waters pushed the whales' food deeper.
stories.stand: An expedition from October 2025 to July 2026 failed to find a single blue whale to tag, as El Niño warmed the waters.
body: A nine-month expedition to tag blue whales around the Galápagos Islands found none, Live Science and Gizmodo reported on 2 November. The search ran from October 2025 to July 2026.
It was led by Daniela Alarcón of Universidad San Francisco de Quito and the Galápagos Science Center. Reported sightings had already fallen in August and September 2025.
Water at 100 metres was up to 5C warmer than usual for the season during an El Niño event, according to Live Science. The researchers suspect the whales moved south to cooler, richer waters.
The team says it is too early to blame El Niño for certain. In September 2026, a citizen science network reported an adult blue whale with a calf off San Cristóbal.

stories.say: Italian researchers in Ethiopia watched a bull named Achille and a male donkey named Patroclo mount each other 51 times in two weeks, alongside licking and nuzzling.
stories.stand: University of Pisa scientists describe a selective sexual and social bond between two males of different species in Current Biology.
body: Researchers from the University of Pisa have described a lasting socio-sexual bond between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau. The study was published in Current Biology on 2 November.
The team recorded 51 mountings between the bull, Achille, and the donkey, Patroclo, between 6 and 19 March 2026. The animals had different owners and met only in the pasture.

Both animals had access to other partners, including their own species, the researchers said. The lead author, Martina Francesconi, said the study could not show what function the behaviour served.

stories.say: Yale researchers say some Caribbean anole lizards have raised their heat tolerance by about 2C in a decade, while species able to dodge the heat have barely changed.
stories.stand: A PNAS study of 16 anole species found forest-canopy lizards adapted fastest to rising temperatures.
body: Some Caribbean lizards are evolving greater tolerance of heat, but at very different rates, according to a Yale-led study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The team compared 16 anole species on Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico, using data from 2011 to 2013 and from 2022 to 2025. They measured the highest temperature each species could tolerate.
Species deep in closed forest canopies raised their heat tolerance by about 2C in a decade, Yale said. Species in open habitats changed little, as they could move to cooler spots.
The lead author, Saúl Domínguez-Guerrero, warned that there is a limit beyond which bodies can no longer adapt. Tests on offspring checked whether the change could be inherited.

body: The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington opened a new gallery, At Home in Space, on 30 October. It covers more than 50 years of people living and working in space.

stories.stand: State health officials said on Monday a child in Lewis County had died during an outbreak that has reached 178 cases this year.
body: A child in Lewis County, in northern New York state, has died after contracting measles, state health officials said on Monday. It is the state's first known measles-associated death in more than 30 years.
The child's age and vaccination status were not given. New York had recorded 178 measles cases this year as of 24 October, 170 of them outside New York City and 8 in the city.
Governor Kathy Hochul said she was heartbroken. She declared a state disaster emergency over the outbreak in October, widening who can give measles jabs.
The state health department said vaccination was the best protection. It is offering MMR vaccines to unvaccinated people who ask, and has sent extra resources to Lewis County.

body: A resident of Yakima County, Washington, has died of H5N1 bird flu after being exposed to infected cattle at a dairy, local health officials said. The person had underlying health conditions and had been in hospital.
It is the first US bird flu death this year and the third since the virus was found in dairy cattle in 2024. The person has not been named.

stories.stand: Ministers say 125 new CT and MRI scanners and AI software have added about one million scans a year in England.
body: The NHS in England added 125 CT and MRI scanners between March 2024 and March 2026, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Tuesday. It says they deliver about one million extra scans a year.
Of the new machines, 107 went to community diagnostic centres. Those centres carried out nearly 2.2 million scans in the year to March 2026, according to NHS England imaging data.
AI software that speeds up MRI scans is now fitted to 54% of compatible NHS scanners. The department said it lets services carry out 14% more scans on average.
Health minister Karin Smyth said quick diagnosis could make all the difference for cancer patients. The scanners are used to diagnose lung, brain, breast and prostate cancers among other conditions.

body: The US Food and Drug Administration has given tentative approval to a generic version of lenacapavir, an injection given twice a year to prevent HIV. It was developed by India's Dr Reddy's Laboratories.
Tentative approval is the standard status for a generic while the original drug is still under patent, according to Unitaid. Gilead's brand-name version was approved in the US in June 2025.
The generic will cost $40 per person a year in the 120 low- and middle-income countries covered by Gilead's voluntary licence. Unitaid said first supplies should reach countries by the end of 2026.
Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI backed the work. More than 125,000 people in Africa have already started on Gilead's version, Unitaid said.

stories.head: Newcastle hospital trust admits baby would have lived if mother kept in

stories.stand: The trust admitted a breach of duty after a woman with pre-eclampsia was sent home against a consultant's advice and her baby died.
body: Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust has admitted a breach of duty over the death of a baby in 2023. It accepted the girl would have survived had her mother not been discharged.

The mother was seven months pregnant when she was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia at the Royal Victoria Infirmary. One consultant advised she stay until the birth, but another reviewed her and she was sent home on 14 February.
She returned the next day with new concerns and staff could not find a heartbeat. The baby had died at around 29 weeks. The family has received an undisclosed settlement.
Ian Joy, the trust's director of nursing and midwifery, apologised and said aspects of care fell short. The trust said it had since improved urgent assessment and escalation.

stories.head: Congo Ebola death toll revised up to 5,372 as fatality rate tops 50%
stories.say: A data correction has pushed Congo's Ebola death toll to 5,372, with more than half of confirmed patients dying, as Africa CDC says most new cases come from unknown chains.
stories.stand: A retrospective correction lifted the death toll to 5,372, and the case fatality rate is now above 50%, official figures show.
body: The Democratic Republic of Congo has recorded 5,372 deaths in its Ebola outbreak, according to the latest report from the national biomedical research institute, INRB.
The sharp rise came from a retrospective correction of data in Ituri province, not a single day's surge, Africanews reported. The case fatality rate is 51.6%.
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Africa CDC says about 80% of new cases are not linked to known contacts.
Cases have also been recorded in Uganda and Kenya, which have each reported two deaths, Al Jazeera said. Trials of the Ervebo vaccine, used against another strain, have begun in Congo.

stories.head: About 7% of US measles patients were misdiagnosed at first, study finds
stories.say: Researchers at the University of Iowa say about 7% of measles patients who sought care were misdiagnosed at least once, mostly in outpatient clinics, raising the risk of spread.
stories.stand: A University of Iowa study of 4,651 US cases found delays averaged just over four days, mostly in outpatient care.
body: About 6.9% of US measles patients who sought medical care were misdiagnosed at least once before being correctly diagnosed, a University of Iowa study has found.
The researchers used insurance records to identify 4,651 cases from 2001 to 2023. They estimated 381 missed chances to recognise the disease, with an average delay of just over four days.

Most delays, 81%, happened in outpatient settings. Children under two and patients given antibiotics for respiratory symptoms were more likely to be missed. The study is in Infection Control and Hospital Epidemiology.
The authors said delays can help the virus spread in waiting rooms. The CDC has counted 4,852 US cases this year as of 29 October.

stories.head: Africa's first trial of a long-acting malaria prevention jab begins in Rwanda
stories.say: A trial of MMV371, an injection designed to protect against malaria for months, has begun in Rwanda, the first such early-stage study of a long-acting jab in Africa.
stories.stand: Medicines for Malaria Venture and Rwanda's Rinda Ubuzima are testing MMV371 in adults and adolescents.
body: A Phase 1b trial of MMV371, a long-acting injection for malaria prevention, has begun in Rwanda, Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) said on Monday. It is the first such trial in Africa.
The study, run with the Rwandan research group Rinda Ubuzima, involves adults and adolescents. It will test safety and tolerability, explore efficacy and track how the body processes the drug.
Earlier research in healthy adults in the UK found the drug was well tolerated and suggested protection for about three months, MMV said. The aim is one injection to cover a whole malaria season.

stories.head: Canberra drug-checking service finds vet sedative in fake Xanax pill
stories.say: Canberra's drug-checking service has found the veterinary sedative medetomidine for the first time, in a pill made to look like Xanax, and warns naloxone cannot reverse it.
stories.stand: CanTEST found medetomidine in a green pill resembling an alprazolam tablet and warned of overdose risk.
body: CanTEST, Canberra's public drug-checking service, has detected the veterinary sedative medetomidine for the first time, ABC News reported. It was in a green rectangular pill resembling a Xanax tablet.
The person who brought it in expected a benzodiazepine or MDMA. The service issued an alert describing medetomidine as a potent sedative that is neither an opioid nor a benzodiazepine.

CanTEST warned that mixing it with alcohol or other drugs sharply raises overdose risk, and that naloxone cannot reverse its effects. The Victorian Pill Service found the drug in fake benzodiazepines earlier this year.

stories.head: Avoidable deaths in England fall to lowest rate on record
stories.say: England's rate of avoidable deaths fell 3.1% in 2025 to its lowest on record, the ONS says, but people in the poorest areas still die avoidably at nearly four times the rate.
stories.stand: Official figures show 110,804 avoidable deaths among under-75s in England in 2025, with a wide gap between rich and poor areas.
body: The rate of avoidable deaths in England fell to 219.5 per 100,000 people in 2025, the lowest on record, the Office for National Statistics said on Monday. That was 3.1% down on 2024.
Avoidable deaths are those among under-75s that could have been prevented or treated. England recorded 110,804, or 20.7% of all registered deaths. Wales had 8,011, with a rate down 0.8%.
Cancers were the largest cause, followed by heart and circulatory disease. The rate fell in every English region.
Men in the most deprived areas of England had a rate of 547.8 per 100,000, against 144.7 in the least deprived, about 3.8 times higher.

stories.head: Older women sold unproven 'three-parent IVF' abroad, STAT investigation finds
stories.say: A STAT investigation says clinics abroad have sold mitochondrial replacement therapy to older women as a fertility fix, though scientists say there is little evidence it works.
stories.stand: STAT says women travelled to clinics in Albania, Mexico, the Bahamas and elsewhere for a technique experts say is unproven for age-related infertility.
body: A STAT News investigation says a for-profit industry has marketed mitochondrial replacement therapy, known as three-parent IVF, to older women with age-related infertility. The technique was developed to prevent inherited mitochondrial disease.
Reporters spoke to 45 patients, doctors, clinic operators and researchers. Women in their late 40s and early 50s travelled to clinics in Albania, Mexico, the Bahamas and the Philippines, STAT said.

A US facilitator, International Fertility Group of North America, raised its package price from $20,000 to $30,000 this year. It removed success-rate claims after STAT's questions, and says it does not guarantee outcomes.

Scientists quoted said evidence that faulty mitochondria cause age-related infertility is sparse. The procedure is effectively barred in the US, and Europe's fertility society ESHRE opposes it as a commercial treatment.

stories.head: COP31 opens in Antalya next week with finance and fossil fuels on the table
stories.say: The UN climate summit in Antalya runs from the ninth to the twentieth of November, with Türkiye as host and Australia leading the negotiations; the US is not expected to attend.
stories.stand: Türkiye hosts the UN climate summit from 9 to 20 November, while Australia runs the negotiations under an unusual shared arrangement.
body: The COP31 UN climate summit takes place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November. Türkiye holds the presidency and runs the action agenda, while Australia leads the negotiations.

Climate Home News said the US is not expected to attend. Leaders expected include Brazil's Lula da Silva, Spain's Pedro Sánchez, Australia's Anthony Albanese and China's vice-premier Ding Xuexiang. A leaders' summit is planned for 11 and 12 November.

Key issues include the scope of a just transition mechanism agreed in Belém, adaptation finance and next steps on moving away from fossil fuels, according to Carbon Brief. Parties disagree on whether a work programme on cutting emissions should continue.

Carbon Brief said 150 parties, covering about three-quarters of global emissions, have submitted new national climate plans. Türkiye is expected to launch a pledge on 10 November to raise electricity's share of final energy use to 35% by 2035.

stories.head: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall in Andhra Pradesh near Ongole
stories.say: Cyclone Murasu came ashore near Ongole in Andhra Pradesh early on Tuesday, with winds gusting to 120 kilometres an hour, less than a week after Cyclone Arnab hit the same state.
stories.stand: The severe cyclonic storm crossed the south Andhra Pradesh coast early on Tuesday, uprooting trees and damaging power lines.
body: Severe cyclonic storm Murasu crossed the south Andhra Pradesh coast close to Ongole in Prakasam district early on Tuesday. The India Meteorological Department said landfall took place between 3:30 and 5:30 am local time.
Winds reached 100 to 110 km/h, gusting to 120 km/h, the IMD said. It warned of a storm surge of 1 to 1.5 metres in low-lying areas, highest in Bapatla, Krishna and Prakasam districts.

Trees were uprooted and electricity poles damaged, the Press Trust of India reported, and crops and fishing boats were hit. National Disaster Response Force teams helped move people to safety. No deaths had been reported in early accounts.
The IMD expected the storm to weaken through Tuesday. It is the second cyclone to strike Andhra Pradesh in about a week, after Cyclone Arnab came ashore on 28 October.

stories.head: Record river levels as floods hit US Southwest before election day
stories.say: Flooding across Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico pushed rivers to record heights at the weekend, forcing evacuations and leaving Colorado officials to rearrange voting for Tuesday.
stories.stand: An atmospheric river drove rivers in Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico to record levels, forcing evacuations in at least a dozen counties.
body: A powerful atmospheric river brought heavy rain to the US Southwest from Friday into Monday. Evacuations spanned at least a dozen counties in Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico, CNN reported.

AccuWeather said 10 river gauges had set record heights by Monday morning. The Gila River near Solomon, Arizona, reached 26.86 feet, beating a 1983 record by more than 6 feet. Flagstaff had 3.37 inches of rain on 1 November, its wettest November day in records going back to 1898.

Two men were found dead in Flagstaff on Monday, CNN reported; one had reportedly fallen into floodwater. AccuWeather reported a death in Henderson, Nevada, on Friday. Arizona Governor Katie Hobbs declared a statewide emergency.
In Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a voting centre and ballot drop box were moved. Flood-hit voters could request emergency ballots or vote elsewhere, but only in statewide races if outside their county.

stories.head: More than 500 academics urge Albanese to stop new fossil fuel projects
stories.say: More than 500 academics have written to Anthony Albanese, saying Australia cannot credibly lead on climate abroad while it expands coal and gas at home, days before COP31.
stories.stand: An open letter to the Australian prime minister calls for a binding timetable to phase out coal, oil and gas ahead of the Antalya summit.
body: More than 500 academics have signed an open letter to Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, sent a week before the COP31 climate summit in Antalya. AAP put the number of Australian-based signatories at 503.

The letter calls for a binding timetable to phase out coal, oil and gas and a halt to new or expanded fossil fuel projects. It names the Hunter Valley Operations mine extension in New South Wales and Beetaloo gas expansion in the Northern Territory.
It argues Australia cannot credibly lead on climate abroad while expanding coal and gas at home, AAP reported. Australia's Chris Bowen will be president of negotiations at COP31.
Signatories include Lesley Hughes of the Climate Change Authority, Climate Analytics founder Bill Hare and climate scientist David Karoly. AAP did not report a government response.

stories.head: Californians vote on measure to fast-track environmental reviews
stories.say: Californians vote on Tuesday on Proposition 45, which would set deadlines for environmental reviews of housing, clean energy and other projects; opponents say it weakens a key law.
stories.stand: Proposition 45 would rewrite the California Environmental Quality Act to speed reviews of projects developers deem essential.
body: California voters decide on Tuesday on Proposition 45, a measure placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce. It would amend the California Environmental Quality Act, known as CEQA.

The measure sets a 365-day limit on environmental reviews for projects developers designate as essential, such as housing, water, transport and wildfire mitigation. Courts would have to rule on challenges within 270 days, CalMatters reported.

Inside Climate News said oil and gas facilities, nuclear power and high-speed rail are excluded. Supporters have spent at least $36 million and opponents about $30 million, it said, citing state records.

Backers say CEQA is outdated and fuels frivolous lawsuits. Opponents, including the Sierra Club and the California Labor Federation, say it would weaken protections. A PPIC poll in October found 50% opposed and 46% in favour.

stories.head: South Africa's first gas power tender ends with no bidder chosen
stories.say: South Africa's first tender for gas-fired power has ended without a single preferred bidder, after none of four bids met requirements, mainly over gas supply guarantees.
stories.stand: Four bids totalling 2,830MW all failed mandatory criteria, but the energy minister says the government is not retreating from gas-to-power.
body: South Africa's first bid window for gas-fired independent power producers ended with no preferred bidders, the Department of Electricity and Energy said. It sought about 2,000MW of capacity.

Four bids totalling 2,830MW were received in May. None met the mandatory criteria, mainly because bidders could not give the required gas supply assurances, the department said. South Africa imports most of its gas from Mozambique and has no LNG terminal.
Minister Kgosientsho Ramokgopa said the country was not retreating from its gas-to-power goals. The department plans consultations and further information before the end of 2026.
In a Daily Maverick analysis, energy analyst Chris Yelland said the grid operator's latest outlook assumes new gas from 2032 and that its results should be treated with caution.

body: Russia has agreed to work with Ghana on a 2,000-megawatt nuclear power plant, Ghana's Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said on 31 October, according to Pulse Ghana.

The commitment followed talks between President John Mahama and President Vladimir Putin at the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow. Mahama had said Ghana had begun discussions with Russia's state nuclear company, Rosatom, on its first nuclear power station.
Ablakwa said the plant would guarantee energy security. No cost, site or construction timeline has been given, and it is not clear whether a formal agreement was signed.
At the same summit, Russian aluminium producer Rusal signed a deal with Ghana to develop a bauxite mine and an alumina refinery, Africanews reported.

stories.head: Kazakhstan releases second Amur tiger into the wild
stories.say: A male Amur tiger has been released into Kazakhstan's Ile-Balkhash reserve, the second in a programme to bring tigers back more than 70 years after they vanished from the country.
stories.stand: A male tiger named Amur was released on 31 October, joining a female freed in July, as Kazakhstan tries to restore tigers to the Balkhash region.
body: Kazakhstan released a male Amur tiger, named Amur, into the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve on 31 October. He wears a satellite collar so specialists can follow his movements.

He is the second tiger released. A female, Umit, was freed in late July and is reported to be adapting well. Two cubs brought from Russia with the adults remain in supervised care and will be released later.

The four tigers came from Russia's Khabarovsk region in May, where they were caught in the wild. The Turan, or Caspian, tiger once lived in the Balkhash region but died out in Kazakhstan in the mid-20th century.
Amur tigers were chosen because genetic research shows they are closely related to the Turan tiger, the Astana Times reported. WWF has supported habitat and prey restoration in the area.

stories.head: Warming halted the start of a new ice age, Baffin Island study suggests
stories.say: Scientists studying a Canadian ice cap say it began growing about 2,000 years ago, in what may have been the start of a new ice age, until warming reversed it around 1960.
stories.stand: A study of the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island, published in Science, suggests glaciation had begun before human-caused warming stopped it.
body: A study of the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island in northern Canada suggests a new glaciation had begun before human-caused warming halted it. It was published in the journal Science, ScienceAlert reported.

The team, led by geochemist Nicolás Young of Columbia University, dated rocks and buried plants at the ice margin. They found the ice cap, a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began growing again about 2,000 years ago.

The ice cap reached its maximum around 1960 and has since shrunk, Euronews reported. Its recent losses can be explained almost entirely by rising summer temperatures, ScienceAlert said. Models suggest it could disappear under current conditions.

body: The 64MW Alabat wind farm in Quezon province, the Philippines, has been energised and is sending power to the Luzon grid, the Daily Tribune reported on Tuesday. Three turbines are generating so far.

stories.head: North Korea denies FBI claim it stole more than $6bn from Binance
stories.say: North Korea has called American claims that its hackers stole more than six billion dollars from the crypto exchange Binance absurd rhetoric and a grave political provocation.
stories.stand: Kim Yo Jong rejected the FBI's attribution of the record Binance theft to a North Korean state hacking unit.
body: North Korea has denied that it was behind the theft of more than $6 billion in crypto assets from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange. The FBI blamed the attack at the weekend on TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit.

In a statement carried by state media on Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, called the US claim absurd rhetoric and a grave political provocation. She said the FBI wanted to brand North Korea a cyber criminal state, and warned of unspecified issues to reconsider.

The FBI said it had seen the hackers converting the stolen assets into ethereum and expected further laundering. Australia's ABC put the loss at $6.3 billion and called it the largest crypto heist on record.

Binance briefly suspended withdrawals, then reopened them on Sunday. It said it had covered most of the stolen assets with company money. Between 06:00 and 15:30 UTC on Sunday, net outflows were about $3.64 billion, ABC reported.
