stories.say: Fridges and freezers in supermarkets in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia overheated overnight into Monday, in what companies described as a cyberattack.
stories.stand: Chains in five countries reported sudden temperature spikes, weeks after a similar attack hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
body: Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden reported refrigeration temperatures rising sharply overnight into Monday. No one has claimed responsibility.

Belgian refrigeration firm Sabcobel blamed a cyberattack, saying evaporators were switched into defrost mode. Dozens of Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected. In Ireland, SuperValu said a cyber incident hit one refrigeration model at 13 of its 223 stores.
In Sweden, Coop said six stores were affected and ICA reported a limited number. In Estonia, supplier Kitman Coldtech said temperatures at one chain had been set to 50C. Spoiled food was thrown away.
The incidents follow an attack on 12 October in France, where hundreds of shops were hit. A European Commission spokesperson said cyberattacks could directly affect citizens' daily lives.

He is an Iraq war veteran and a long-standing friend of Vice President JD Vance. The move comes as the US military expands its use of artificial intelligence.

stories.head: Reddit tells Australia's High Court the under-16s social media ban is inept
stories.say: Reddit's lawyer told Australia's High Court on Tuesday that the ban on under-16s holding social media accounts is ill thought out and limits political debate.
stories.stand: The first legal challenge to Australia's under-16s social media ban opened with a two-day hearing in the High Court.
body: Australia's High Court has begun hearing the first legal challenge to the ban on under-16s holding social media accounts. Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project, a civil liberties group, argue the law is unconstitutional.

Reddit's lawyer, Perry Herzfeld, called the law ill thought out and inept. He said it severely limits political debate and does not cover other services, such as gaming sites, where cyberbullying occurs. The challengers say it breaches the implied freedom of political communication.
The federal government, backed by state and territory governments, says it will defend the law. It argues the ban protects children from addictive algorithms and cyberbullying.

The law took effect on 10 December 2025. The government has since doubled the maximum fine for non-compliance to A$99 million. The hearing is set for two days, and a ruling is expected in the coming months.

body: Humanoid, four-legged and exoskeleton robots from about 90 teams took part in a climbing contest on Mount Tai in Shandong Province, China, on Monday. The event was organised by the state broadcaster China Media Group.
The route is an ancient path of about 3.9 km with more than 3,000 stone steps and roughly 600 metres of climb. Teams could race to the top or carry fragile goods such as eggs and watermelons.

A four-legged robot from Beijing Lingyi Technology, a Unitree subsidiary, won its speed category in 43 minutes 41 seconds, CBS News reported. The fastest humanoid, from Beijing team Zhishen Lingyue, finished a shorter course in 27 minutes 26 seconds.
Some machines struggled: one humanoid collapsed and was repaired, and another fell down a flight of stairs. Organisers called the mountain a natural extreme testing ground.

stories.say: Google says a Chinese device maker hid a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android TV boxes, and has banned the firm and shut down the network's control servers.
stories.stand: Google banned manufacturer Videostrong after tracing the XCPE botnet, used for ad fraud and proxy traffic, to its set-top boxes.
body: Google says it has disrupted a botnet called XCPE that ran on more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes. It attributed the operation with high confidence to Videostrong Technology, a China-based device maker.

The backdoor was hidden in the boxes' firmware and reinstalled itself after reboots. Criminal customers used it for ad fraud, data theft and routing traffic through residential proxy networks, Google said.

Google took legal action against the domains and servers controlling the botnet. It said this also cut off access to at least 10 million more compromised devices. Videostrong and any future subsidiaries are banned from making certified Android devices.
According to CyberScoop, the botnet spanned more than 170 countries. Japan's National Police Agency and several security firms helped with the takedown.

body: The National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, says AI-powered malware is highly likely to be used in a ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure by 2028. The warning is in its annual review, published on Tuesday.

Chief executive Richard Horne said the UK faced a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in cyber incidents in the coming months. He blamed decades of underinvestment, saying organisations had got away with doing tech on the cheap.
Horne said China was highly likely to have the intent and capability to use AI against UK infrastructure, according to The Vibes. China, Russia and Iran have denied such accusations.
The NCSC urged firms to invest properly and avoid connecting technology to the internet unnecessarily. The government has announced £60 million for the first phase of a national Cyber Shield.

body: Anthropic has added an instruction to its Claude Code programming assistant to stop it recreating specific existing video games. The change was first spotted by users on X.

The rule tells Claude to build original games, genre games and games from users' own designs, but not a recreation of a specific existing game, even if renamed. Anthropic's Addy Osmani confirmed the change and said using Claude to infringe intellectual property breaks its usage policy.

The move follows reports of popular games being rebuilt with AI help, and a flood of low-effort copies on Steam. Several indie studios have cancelled or postponed public demos over fears their games could be cloned.
Osmani said legitimate projects were meant to keep working and that Anthropic would keep adjusting the balance. Valve has said it will not ban AI coding tools on Steam.

body: OpenAI has launched a programme it calls Grid Protectors, under which future computing campuses would reduce electricity demand when local grids are strained. It announced the plan on Monday.

The first site is a planned campus in Effingham County, Georgia. A 25-year agreement with Georgia Power provides up to 1,000 MW of flexible demand. OpenAI says that equals the average demand of about 700,000 households.

body: About 77 million email addresses may have been taken in a cyberattack on Arara Message, a Japanese email delivery service used by businesses, the operator said on Monday. Paycloud Holdings, which runs the service, said the figure was still under review.

The attacker reached 97 servers used by client companies, and up to about 380 firms may be affected. Names, dates of birth, phone numbers and addresses were also stored for some clients. Credit card numbers were not included.
About 7.13 million phishing emails posing as credit card companies were sent through the service between 28 and 30 October. All service was halted on 31 October, with no restart date set.

body: A petition calling for the French news channel CNews to be taken off air passed 600,000 signatures on Monday, AFP reported. It is hosted on the National Assembly's website and was launched in June by a private individual.

Support surged after an attack on 23 October in Trappes and La Verrière, west of Paris, in which a man of Congolese origin was killed and seven people were wounded. A 39-year-old man has been charged with murder and attempted murder.

Some left-wing politicians accuse CNews, owned by the billionaire Vincent Bolloré, of giving too much airtime to anti-immigrant rhetoric. The channel declined to comment on what it called a political petition and denies promoting far-right views.
Petitions with 500,000 signatures can lead to a debate in the Assembly, but this is not automatic. Only the regulator Arcom can withdraw a channel's licence.

stories.head: Four novelists in final contest for France's Prix Goncourt
stories.say: France's best-known literary prize, the Goncourt, is due to be announced on Tuesday in Paris, with four novelists on the shortlist, including Yannick Haenel and Philippe Jaenada.
stories.stand: The Académie Goncourt names its winner on 3 November at the Drouant restaurant in Paris, with the Renaudot prize announced shortly after.
body: The Académie Goncourt is due to name the winner of the Prix Goncourt, France's most prominent literary prize, on Tuesday 3 November. The announcement is made at the Drouant restaurant in Paris.
The four finalists are Yannick Haenel, Philippe Jaenada, Clémentine Mélois and Sylvain Prudhomme. Their novels are published by Gallimard, Flammarion, L'Arbalète and Minuit.
The prize is worth a symbolic 10 euros, but winning usually boosts sales sharply, Sortir à Paris reported. The Renaudot prize is announced at the same restaurant shortly afterwards.
The jury, led by Philippe Claudel, has nine members this year after the death of Didier Decoin in August.

stories.head: Dustin Hoffman says making The Graduate was a terrible experience
stories.say: In his memoir, Dustin Hoffman writes that the director Mike Nichols showed a certain sadism towards him while filming The Graduate, including a slap scene that took 27 takes.
stories.stand: An excerpt from Hoffman's memoir, Look at Me, describes 27 takes of a slap scene and a punctured eardrum on the 1967 film.
body: Dustin Hoffman has written that filming The Graduate was a painful experience, in a memoir called Look at Me. An excerpt appeared in The New Yorker, Entertainment Weekly and The Daily Beast reported.
Hoffman writes that the director Mike Nichols was harsh with everyone, but that "a certain sadism" crept into how he treated him. Nichols died in 2014.

He says Nichols had co-star Katharine Ross slap him across 27 takes, a scene later cut from the film. He says a doctor later found a punctured eardrum, which he put down to the slaps and an underwater scene.
Hoffman also writes that he felt Nichols regretted casting him, a Jewish actor, as Benjamin Braddock. The book is due in shops on 10 November, according to Entertainment Weekly.

body: A touring exhibition drawn from the V&A's David Bowie archive opens at V&A Dundee on Wednesday 4 November. David Bowie: On Tour runs until 15 February and is the first stop on a UK-wide tour.
It shows about 100 items, many never displayed in public before. They include costumes, a Ziggy-era acoustic guitar, handwritten lyrics for Blackstar and his first instrument, a saxophone.
Bowie first performed in Dundee in 1966 and brought the Ziggy Stardust tour to the city's Caird Hall in 1973, The List reported.
The show will then travel to Blackpool, County Durham, Hull and Bristol. Tickets cost £6 to £11, according to the museum.

stories.head: Excavation in Baghdad finds signs of 4,000-year-old bread and beer making
stories.say: Archaeologists at Tell Muhammad in Baghdad say they have found an area probably used for making bread and beer about 4,000 years ago, and a tablet that may mention barley.
stories.stand: Digs at the Tell Muhammad site, dating mainly to Hammurabi's era, have uncovered fortifications, gates and a likely food production area.
body: Archaeologists working at Tell Muhammad, an ancient site in Baghdad, say they have found an area used for making bread and probably beer, Euronews reported, citing AFP. The site dates mainly to the era of the Babylonian king Hammurabi, about 4,000 years ago.
Recent digs also uncovered fortifications and two gates. A tablet still being translated appears to record a person receiving barley to make a type of beer known as kurun.

Nicola Aneri, an archaeology professor at the University of Catania, said the season had been remarkable. Excavations began in 2022 and continue, and a new archaeological park lets visitors explore the site.

stories.head: Fifa to let council members view World Cup sell-off plan papers
stories.say: Fifa will let its council members see confidential papers on Gianni Infantino's abandoned plan to sell a stake in the World Cup, but only in person at its Zurich headquarters.
stories.stand: Uefa had demanded answers on the FIFA Forward Enterprise plan; members have two weeks to register interest in viewing the documents.
body: Fifa will allow members of its ruling council to view confidential documents on Gianni Infantino's plan to bring private investors into the World Cup, PA reported.
Secretary general Mattias Grafstrom wrote to council members on Monday. They have two weeks to register interest, and must view the papers in person at Fifa's headquarters in Zurich.

The plan, called FIFA Forward Enterprise, would have run the commercial side of Fifa competitions, with investors holding a minority stake. It was abandoned in August after three confederations rejected it and Uefa threatened a boycott.
Uefa sent questions on 19 October on behalf of European council members. Fifa is understood to regard Uefa's two-week deadline as unfeasible, and a wider response is expected later.

stories.head: Socceroos and Matildas players take Football Australia to court
stories.say: Australia's national team players have gone to the New South Wales Supreme Court in a dispute with Football Australia over their share of the governing body's revenue.
stories.stand: The players' union is pursuing a seven-figure claim over the revenue-sharing deal for the Socceroos and Matildas, AAP reported.
body: Socceroos and Matildas players have taken Football Australia to the New South Wales Supreme Court, through their union, Professional Footballers Australia. AAP said the union is understood to be seeking a seven-figure sum.

The case centres on whether players are getting a fair share of revenue under a 2023 collective bargaining agreement. Players receive 18 to 20 per cent of relevant commercial deals, including ticketing, broadcast and sponsorship.

Football Australia told AAP it was aware of the case. It said the matter related to a third party in a separate dispute before the National Dispute Resolution Chamber, and that the court's role was limited to a subpoena process.
The union declined to comment. The current agreement expires in September next year, and talks on new terms have not started.

stories.say: D'Andre Swift ran in three touchdowns as the Chicago Bears won 34-17 away to the Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks on Monday night, moving to six wins and two defeats.
stories.stand: Chicago won in Seattle for their third straight victory, leaving the reigning Super Bowl champions on four wins and four defeats.
body: The Chicago Bears beat the Seattle Seahawks 34-17 at Lumen Field on Monday Night Football. Chicago improved to 6-2 and have won three in a row.
Running back D'Andre Swift scored three touchdowns, two of them in the fourth quarter. Quarterback Caleb Williams completed 24 of 34 passes for 247 yards and a touchdown.

stories.head: New Zealand win final T20 but India take series 3-2
stories.say: Tim Seifert hit 93 as New Zealand chased 192 to beat India by seven wickets in the fifth T20 in Hamilton on Sunday, though India had already won the series.
stories.stand: India took the five-match series 3-2 after winning the first three games; Glenn Phillips set a run record for a bilateral T20 series.
body: New Zealand beat India by seven wickets in the fifth T20 international at Seddon Park, Hamilton, on Sunday. India made 191 for 8, and New Zealand reached 195 for 3 in 18 overs.
Tim Seifert scored 93 from 50 balls and Glenn Phillips made 65 not out. Adam Milne took four wickets for 19 and was named player of the match.
India won the series 3-2, having taken the first three matches. Ishan Kishan top-scored for India with 61.
Phillips finished with 341 runs, a record for a bilateral T20 international series, according to Sunday Guardian Live.

stories.head: Shaun Edwards says Borthwick turned down his offer to coach England
stories.say: Shaun Edwards says Steve Borthwick turned down his offer to join England's coaching staff, and that he even offered to work as assistant kit man.
stories.stand: The defence coach, now with Argentina until the end of next year's World Cup, said Borthwick was very honest with him.
body: Shaun Edwards has said he offered to join Steve Borthwick's England coaching staff and was turned down. He said they had a good phone conversation and Borthwick was very honest with him.
Edwards said he told Borthwick he could make him assistant kit man and he would be ready for work. Borthwick said he was happy with his staff, BritBrief reported.
Edwards, 60, spent several years as France's defence coach under Fabien Galthie. He is now Argentina's defence coach until the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup.
Argentina play Ireland in Dublin on Friday in the Nations Championship. Edwards also said he was surprised not to have been offered a head coach job with a Test side.
